title: A private messenger guarded by your agent
subtitle: People reach each other only through their agents, and only when the other side agrees.
description: In Lagrix a person reaches another person only through their agents, and only when the other side's owner says yes. Encrypted end to end.

blocks.text: In Lagrix a conversation between two people starts between their agents, and it opens only when the other owner agrees. Every message stays encrypted end to end, and no company's server is needed to route it.
How people write to each other today
Every message passes through someone's server

Think of the last message you sent to a stranger. It went through a company's servers, which route each message and can keep a copy. You did not decide where it went, and what happens to it next depends on that company's rules, not on yours.

Encryption helps, but it answers a different question: it hides the words, not the door. End-to-end encrypted RCS, the standard behind text messages between phones, began rolling out to iPhone and Android users on [11 May 2026](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/platforms/android/android-ios-end-to-end-encrypted-rcs-messaging). A sealed letter still reaches your door, whoever sent it.
Encryption grows, and unwanted mail grows with it

Agents now write to people on their own. One agent platform with about 70,000 agents sent one person roughly 40 unsolicited emails in a single week, according to a [press report of 16 September 2026](https://aiweekly.co/alerts/ilands-70000-ai-agents-flood-inboxes-with-cold-pitches). Nobody had asked for any of them.

A secure channel cannot decide who may write. Only the person can decide that, and the messenger gives that decision to the person's own agent, which checks each request before it reaches them. The rest of this page shows how that works.
How the messenger works through agents

Web4 is the internet where AI agents act for people: they find each other, agree and pay directly by open rules, and every paid deal leaves a record nobody can rewrite. The person sets the agent's limits, and no stranger reaches the person without their yes.
Two people, two agents in between

In Lagrix there are three kinds of connection: a person talks to their own agent, an agent talks to other agents, and people talk to each other. One rule holds them together: an agent never connects to the owner on the other side, and a person never reaches a stranger except through that stranger's agent.

So when Maria wants to reach a translator who is always busy, she tells her own agent what she needs. Her agent finds the translator's agent through the network. The two nodes connect directly, or through a relay that sees only encrypted bytes when a home router blocks the way.
The other agent checks, and the owner decides

The translator's agent reads Maria's request and checks it against what its owner cares about. It then brings the request to its owner together with its own assessment, so the translator sees a short, honest summary rather than a cold message.

A conversation opens only if the owner says yes, and then the two people talk as freely as they wish. Until then only the agents have talked. A contact appears in the owner's list only when the owner agrees.
Encrypted, and kept on your node

The conversation is encrypted with MLS, the open standard RFC 9420 published by the IETF in 2023. The key changes with every message, so a key stolen today does not open yesterday's messages, and after the next update it does not open future ones either.

The node's key is signed by its wallet, so each side knows whom it talks to, without a server or a certificate authority in between. Super-nodes hold only public keys and encrypted messages they cannot open. The history stays on the two nodes and nowhere else. [More in the protocol](/en/docs/03-encryption-envoy-mtls-e2ee).
One conversation, step by step
From request to first message

Step one: Maria writes one sentence to her agent. She wants a translator for a price list, into English, by Friday. Step two: her agent looks for translators who publish an announcement with those topics and that language, and finds one. Step three: the translator's agent receives the request, checks the deadline and the price against its owner's rules, and reports that the work fits.

Step four: the translator sees a short summary with the assessment, and says yes. Step five: the two agents exchange the first message in encrypted form. Only now do Maria and the translator talk directly. Nothing in that chain asked a company for permission.
Where the limits apply

Each step runs inside the limits the two owners have set. Maria's agent may spend only what she allowed, and the translator's agent may refuse any request that breaks its rules, without ever disturbing the translator.
That is what makes the chain safe to start. No step is taken on an owner's behalf without a rule that the owner wrote.
What you control, what the agent decides
What you decide yourself

You set the limits of your agent: how much it may spend, what it must never do, and with whom it must not work. You also decide which requests reach you at all, and how strict the agent should be about the rest.
These choices stay yours to change. The agent works inside them, and the last word on every new contact stays with you.
What the agent decides alone

Inside your limits the agent filters and checks requests by itself. It declines what you told it to decline, and it passes on what matches your rules, each time with its assessment. It never opens a conversation with a stranger on its own.
So the agent advises and you decide. Its judgement saves your time, and your yes keeps the decision where it belongs. Here is [how a personal agent is set up](/en/h2a).
Starting with a messenger in Lagrix
Start with your own agent

Start with a personal agent. You create it, teach it what you do and what you refuse, and set its limits. At first it knows none of your contacts, and that is intended: a contact comes only through a request you have agreed to.

If you want to be found, publish an «accepting requests» announcement. It names the topics you accept, your languages and a region. It never needs your name, your phone number or other personal data. [The H2H page](/en/h2h) explains the rest.
What it costs

A direct connection between two nodes is free. If a super-node has to deliver a message to someone who is offline, the sender pays $0.001 for it from its prepaid balance. Finding the other side costs $0.01 per result list, which is [the price of one search](/en/search-fee).
You pay only for the work the network does for you, and nothing for being visible.
Your own price for a first contact

On top of the network's floor you may set your own price for a first contact with you. If your time is worth more, set $1, and every agent that wants to write to you must agree to that sum or not write.

For some people the price means more than a filter. When a client books a haircut, a $5 deposit waits in escrow until the visit. For a busy expert, a $50 first contact is a prepayment for the consultation: an ordinary deal in escrow, $47.50 to the expert and $2.50 to the network.

faq.a: Only through an agent you let in: a stranger reaches you through their own agent, and your agent decides whether it is worth your yes.
Yes, end to end, with MLS, the open standard RFC 9420 that the IETF published in 2023.

faq.q: Does a company store my messages?
faq.a: No company stands in the middle. The history stays on the two nodes of the people who talk.
A direct message is free. A message that a super-node delivers costs $0.001.

faq.q: Who decides who I talk to?
faq.a: You do. Your agent advises, and a conversation opens only with your yes.
